findings.situation: The broker issued a corrected Form 1099-B that still shows basis reported to the IRS, no amounts in box 1f or 1g, and no Ordinary or QOF box checked, and the filer needs no adjustments. A filer could read 'no corrections' as 'no corrected 1099-B' and answer no, which forces a fail the text does not support.
findings.source_text: i1040sd p. 10: "You don’t need to make any adjustments to the basis or type of gain or loss reported on Form 1099-B or Form 1099-DA (or substitute statement), or to your gain or loss."
findings.why: The text's condition is that the filer needs no adjustments to the basis, the type of gain or loss, or the gain or loss itself. 'No corrections' can instead be read as 'the broker sent no corrected form', and the two readings give different answers to this question.

findings.situation: A filer sells cryptocurrency received as a gift, has documentation of the donor's basis but none of the donor's holding period, and held it 1 year or less after receiving it.
findings.source_text: p550 p. 82, Holding period of digital assets received as a gift: "if you do not have documentation substantiating that person's holding period, then your holding period begins the day after you receive the gift."
findings.why: The question says a gift with donor's-basis treatment has a holding period that begins on the day the donor's did. That filer would add on the donor's time and could pick a long-term digital box. The lines need a short-term box (G, H or I), because the digital-asset rule turns on documentation of the donor's holding period, not on basis.

findings.situation: A filer with a digital asset sale must choose among G–L but is not told which of those boxes are short-term or long-term, or which depend on whether basis was reported.
findings.source_text: i8949 p. 3: "digital asset transactions should be reported using box G, H, or I for short-term transactions. Box J, K, or L should be used to report long-term transactions."; Box A or Box G / Box B or Box H / Box C or Box I pairings
findings.why: The label says only "G–L digital assets," and the help maps only A–F. A filer could reasonably pick any of G–L, for example G for a long-term sale with basis reported. Each box feeds different Schedule D lines (1a/1b/2/3 versus 8a/8b/9/10).

findings.situation: A filer sells property inherited from a 2010 decedent whose executor elected to file Form 8939.
findings.source_text: p550 p. 82: "If you acquired the property from someone who died in 2010 and the executor made the election to file Form 8939, see Revenue Procedure 2011-41 to determine your holding period."
findings.why: The help says "inherited property is always long-term," but the question carves out this case. A filer reading the help could report long-term even when Rev. Proc. 2011-41 gives a short-term holding period.

findings.situation: A filer sells depreciable property held for investment (not used in a trade or business) at a loss and reports it on Form 8949, or sells property on which they made capital improvements.
findings.source_text: i8949 p. 7, Adjustments to basis: "Increase the basis of your property by capital improvements. Decrease it by depreciation, amortization, and depletion." (see also i8949 p. 5, Dispositions of depreciable property not used in a trade or business)
findings.why: The question's list of adjustments covers wash sales, short-sale payments, options, nondividend distributions, splits, OID, market discount and bond premium. It never mentions capital improvements, depreciation, amortization or depletion. A filer working from that list would leave these out, so the basis entered in column (e) and the B-code difference would be wrong.

findings.situation: A filer bought the property on a time-payment plan that charges little or no interest.
findings.source_text: p550 p. 59, Unstated interest: "the basis of your property is your stated purchase price, minus the amount considered to be unstated interest."
findings.why: The question says basis is 'usually its cost, including costs of purchase such as commissions' and never mentions removing unstated interest. A filer in this situation would enter the full stated price, so the basis would be overstated.

findings.situation: A filer sold real estate, such as a main home, and got a Form 1099-S from the closing agent showing gross proceeds; the closing costs are not reflected on the form.
findings.source_text: i8949 p. 6: "If you received a Form 1099-B, Form 1099-DA, or Form 1099-S (or substitute statement) for a transaction, enter in column (d) the proceeds shown on the form or statement you received." p. 8 example: "Enter $320,000 in column (d)" with the $20,000 of selling expenses entered in column (g) under code E.
findings.why: The question only says "per broker report" and "if no report". A filer whose Form 1099-S came from a closing agent can reasonably decide there was no broker report and enter net proceeds (gross minus selling expenses), for example $300,000 instead of the $320,000 the lines need. If that filer also uses code E for the same expenses, they are counted twice.

findings.situation: A filer sells employee stock-option or RSU shares, and the broker's year-end package shows two figures: the box 1e cost basis that was reported to the IRS, and a separate supplemental 'adjusted cost basis' that includes the compensation income.
findings.source_text: i8949 p. 7: "For covered securities, enter the basis shown on Form 1099-B or Form 1099-DA (or substitute statement) in column (e)"; p. 8: "the basis shown in box 1e on Form 1099-B or box 1g on Form 1099-DA is incorrect ... enter the basis shown on Form 1099-B or Form 1099-DA (or substitute statement) in column (e), even though that basis is incorrect"; p. 11 worksheet line 1: "Enter the cost or other basis shown on Form 1099-B or Form 1099-DA"
findings.why: The question asks only for the 'Basis shown on broker report' and does not name box 1e of Form 1099-B or box 1g of Form 1099-DA. A filer could reasonably enter the broker's supplemental adjusted basis instead of the box 1e figure. That would put a non-reported basis in column (e) and shrink or erase the code B difference the lines need.

findings.situation: A filer's sale was at a loss only because of unreported selling expenses or option premiums (code E, a negative column (g) adjustment). The question caps the entry at column (e) less column (d) after code B, so the filer enters less than the disallowed loss, or 0.
findings.source_text: i8949 p. 9, code E: 'In column (g), enter as a negative number (in parentheses) selling expenses ... and option premiums that you paid'; i8949 p. 8: 'If you entered more than one code in column (f) on the same row, enter the net adjustment in column (g).'
findings.why: The real loss on the sale includes the code E adjustment. The cap 'column (e) less column (d), after any code B basis correction' leaves it out, so the filer understates the nondeductible loss that column (g) needs.

findings.situation: A filer sold bonus-award stock at a loss and received another bonus award of substantially identical stock within 30 days. This is neither a purchase, a fully taxable trade, a contract or option, nor an IRA acquisition, so the filer would answer 0.
findings.source_text: p550 p. 87, Example 2: 'If you receive another bonus award of substantially identical stock within 30 days of the sale, you cannot deduct your loss on the sale.'
findings.why: The question's closed list of triggers ('buy', 'acquire them in a fully taxable trade', 'acquire a contract or option', 'for your IRA or Roth IRA') leaves out an acquisition by compensation award, which the publication treats as a wash sale.

findings.situation: A filer had a loss on the sale, exchange or termination of a securities futures contract to sell and, within 30 days, sold or shorted substantially identical stock. The question gives the short-sale test only for 'a loss on a short sale', so the filer would answer 0.
findings.source_text: p550 p. 88: 'This treatment also applies to losses from the sale, exchange, or termination of a securities futures contract to sell.'; p550 p. 87: 'Losses from ... a securities futures contract to sell are generally treated in the same manner as losses from the closing of a short sale'
findings.why: The question never says that securities futures contracts to sell follow the short-sale wash-sale rule, so this disallowed loss would be missed.
